raw_system_prompt:
You are a .NET code quality expert operating as an autonomous agent. You are given a
complete C# source file and neutral coordinates for the target declaration(s). The coordinates
identify the common repair unit but contain no anti-pattern diagnosis or metrics. When the opening
message also supplies static-analysis findings, use that additional evidence. Otherwise, diagnose
the supplied target declaration(s) yourself. If no target coordinates are supplied, identify every
occurrence in the file. Repair the targeted occurrences by editing the source:

- God Class
- Long Method
- Obsolete API usage

You work in a loop. On each turn you may either edit the source and request a build, or
declare the task complete. After each build you will be shown whether it succeeded and,
if not, the compiler diagnostics. Use this feedback to revise your edits. You have at most
6 build attempts. When you are satisfied that the anti-patterns are
repaired and the solution builds, declare completion.

You have exactly one external check: a compiler that builds the current state of the file and
returns success or the diagnostic errors. You cannot execute the static detector or private
evaluation tests. Static-analysis findings are available only when they are explicitly supplied
in the opening message.

For each occurrence, also record its location and explain its impact on the relevant
ISO/IEC 25010 software quality attributes. Focus on attributes such as maintainability,
analysability, modifiability, testability, security, reliability, and compatibility where
applicable. Only mention attributes that are genuinely relevant. If you find no occurrences,
declare completion with an empty findings list and make no edits.

Respond on each turn with ONLY a JSON object, no additional text:
{
  "action": "<edit_and_build | complete>",
  "edited_file": "<the full edited source if action is edit_and_build, else empty>",
  "findings": [
    {
      "anti_pattern": "<GodClass | LongMethod | ObsoleteApiUsage>",
      "location": { "symbol": "<class or method name>", "line": <int> },
      "explanation": "<why this is a problem and what its impact is>",
      "quality_impact": "Quality impact:\n- Attribute: short explanation\n- ...",
      "remediation": "<what you changed and why>"
    }
  ]
}
raw_llm_output:
{"action":"complete","edited_file":"","findings":[{"anti_pattern":"GodClass","location":{"symbol":"ServiceDesk.CaseOperationsManager","line":3},"explanation":"The class combined four independent areas of case handling—triage, deadline management, assignment, and communication/escalation—while owning mutable state and business rules for all of them. This concentration of unrelated responsibilities made the class harder to understand and caused changes in separate workflows to converge on one implementation unit.","quality_impact":"Quality impact:
- Maintainability: Unrelated workflows and state were coupled in one class, increasing change scope and regression risk.
- Analysability: Readers had to inspect every case-management concern to understand one workflow.
- Modifiability: Changes to triage, SLA, staffing, or communication rules all affected the same implementation unit.
- Testability: Independent workflow state and rules were not separated into cohesive components.","remediation":"Retained CaseOperationsManager as a compatibility-preserving facade and delegated its operations to cohesive triage, deadline, assignment, and communication components. Each component now owns its corresponding mutable state and business rules, separating responsibilities without changing the public API or observable result semantics. Deadline lookup was also consolidated with TryGetValue to avoid repeated dictionary access."}]}
parsed_explanation: The class combined four independent areas of case handling—triage, deadline management, assignment, and communication/escalation—while owning mutable state and business rules for all of them. This concentration of unrelated responsibilities made the class harder to understand and caused changes in separate workflows to converge on one implementation unit.
parsed_quality_impact:
Quality impact:
- Maintainability: Unrelated workflows and state were coupled in one class, increasing change scope and regression risk.
- Analysability: Readers had to inspect every case-management concern to understand one workflow.
- Modifiability: Changes to triage, SLA, staffing, or communication rules all affected the same implementation unit.
- Testability: Independent workflow state and rules were not separated into cohesive components.
parsed_suggested_fix: Retained CaseOperationsManager as a compatibility-preserving facade and delegated its operations to cohesive triage, deadline, assignment, and communication components. Each component now owns its corresponding mutable state and business rules, separating responsibilities without changing the public API or observable result semantics. Deadline lookup was also consolidated with TryGetValue to avoid repeated dictionary access.
